'''Bernd Gerhard Würsig''' (born 9 November 1948 in [[Barsinghausen]], Germany)<ref name="BerndGerhard">"Bernd Gerhard Würsig". Marqui's Who's Who in the World. 2012. 29th Edition.</ref> is an educator and researcher who works mainly on aspects of behavior and behavioral ecology of whales and dolphins.<ref name="Cahill">Cahill T. 2000. Dolphins. National Geographic Society, Washington, DC. 216 pp.</ref>  Much of his early work was done in close collaboration with his wife Melany Ann Würsig (born Carballeira),<ref name="Cahill" /> and they have published numerous manuscripts and books together.<ref name="BerndGerhard"/> He is now Professor Emeritus at [[Texas A&M University]], teaching only occasionally but still involved with graduate student and other research. He is especially active with problems and potential solutions concerning Indo-Pacific [[humpback dolphins]], ''Sousa chinensis'', in and surrounding waters of Hong Kong. Würsig has conducted research with marine mammals in several parts of the world, including the South Atlantic, Hawaii, US and Canadian Arctic, New Zealand, the Gulf of Mexico, Hong Kong, the Yangtze River of Central China, the Peruvian Amazon, and the Russian Far East.<ref name="www.dolphinbiology.org-1" />

== Early career and education ==
Bernd Würsig is the youngest of three sons of Gerhard and Charlotte Würsig,<ref name="BerndGerhard" /> Silesian refugees who moved to (then) West Germany after the [[World War II]], and to the United States under a refugee [[family visa]] in 1956.  They settled in Ohio, and Würsig became interested as a boy in marine mammals after reading books by the Austrian explorers [[Hans Hass]] and [[Lotte Hass]], French [[Jacques Cousteau]], and American [[John C. Lilly]].<ref name="Grady">Grady D. 2003. More Grady’s People. Pp. 157-170 “U.S. dolphin professor who loves Kaikoura”. Nikau Press, Nelson, New Zealand.</ref>  He went to [[Ohio State University]], and received a Bachelor of Science degree in zoology (minor in Germanic Literature) in 1971. Würsig went to [[Stony Brook University]] (then the State University of New York at Stony Brook), 1971–1978, in an interdisciplinary Ph.D. program with advisors in the Departments of Marine Science, Ecology and Evolution, and Neurobiology and Behavior. His advisors in the latter two, [[George C. Williams (biologist)|George Williams]] in Ecology and Evolution and Charles Walcott in Neurobiology and Behavior, had a strong influence on Würsig's career, as the former imbued him with a sense of the wonders of animal social/sexual strategies, and the latter with a lifelong appreciation for how to think about animal capabilities, relative to our own capabilities of observation with basic tools such as binoculars to sophisticated radio, theodolite, and other remote sensing techniques. Würsig's field advisor [[Roger Payne]], the discoverer of humpback whale song and long-range communication in fin and blue whales, was his mentor during field work on dolphins in coastal Patagonia, Argentina.<ref name="Cahill" />From 1978 to 1981, Würsig also worked with [[Kenneth S. Norris]]<ref name="Norris">Norris KS. 1994. Introduction. Pp. 1-13 in Norris KS, Würsig B, Wells RS, Würsig M, eds. The Hawaiian Spinner Dolphin. University of California Press, Berkeley, CA.</ref> as a [[National Institutes of Health]] and [[National Science Foundation]] post-doctoral fellow, and then became assistant professor at [[Moss Landing Marine Laboratories]], central California, where he went through the professor ranks in the 1980s, becoming full professor in spring 1989.  That year, he and Melany and their two children Paul and Kim moved to Texas A&M University, where he started the Marine Mammal Research Program (now Marine Mammal Behavioral Ecology Group).<ref name="Cahill" />

== Academic career ==
He joined Texas A&M University in 1989 as a professor of marine biology and wildlife and fisheries sciences. He subsequently developed the university's marine mammal research activities at the Galveston campus and served as director of the Marine Mammal Research Program and later the Marine Mammal Behavioral Ecology Group. He also served as director of the Institute of Marine Life Sciences from 1996 to 2010. Courses associated with his teaching included Biology of Marine Mammals, Cetacean Behavior and Behavioral Ecology, Behavioral Ecology of Marine Mammals and Seabirds of New Zealand, and field-based courses in New Zealand and Greece, dealing with dolphins, fisheries, and conservation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Distinguished Achievement Award Winners |url=https://www.aggienetwork.com/tribute/tributelist/?exhibitId=18&pageNum=9&pageSize=30&sort=yearAwarded&desc=True}}</ref>

He was appointed a Regents Professor of the Texas A&M University System in 2006. The Regents Professorship program recognizes professors for service and contributions at university, state, national, or international levels; Texas A&M's records list Würsig among the system's Regents Professors.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tribute Exhibit |url=https://www.aggienetwork.com/tribute/index/827-18/ |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=www.aggienetwork.com}}</ref>

In 2012, he was appointed to the George P. Mitchell '40 Chair in Sustainable Fisheries. In 2013, Texas A&M University designated him a University Distinguished Professor. The university describes the University Distinguished Professorship as a title recognizing faculty achievement in teaching, mentoring, discovery, and service.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Patterson |first=Shantelle |date=2013-03-08 |title=TAMUG marine biology professor receives Texas A&M University Distinguished Professor Award. |url=https://news.galveston.tamu.edu/2013/03/07/tamug-marine-biology-professor-receives-texas-am-university-distinguished-professor-award/ |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=Texas A&M Galveston Newsroom |language=en-US}}</ref> Würsig became University Distinguished Professor Emeritus in 2016.<ref name="Reference-1" />

Until Spring 2018, Würsig taught undergraduate and graduate courses in aspects of marine mammalogy, specializing in behavior and behavioral ecology.  He has published widely in the popular literature as part of teaching endeavors, such as for the journals [[Natural History (magazine)|Natural History]] and [[Scientific American]], and he has been advisor to numerous movies made for television, as well as the IMAX movie “Dolphins” (2000) that was nominated for an [[Academy Award]], Best Documentary Short Subject.<ref name="Cahill" /> He formerly led field courses on marine bird and mammal biology in Argentina, Mexico, Spain, China, New Zealand, Greece, Alaska, and elsewhere, but as Professor Emeritus does so only occasionally.

== Research ==
Most of Würsig's research, while focused generally on social, sexual, calf rearing, and foraging strategies, has been related to human use of the marine environment, as well as [[tucuxi]] and [[boto]] dolphins of the Amazon and the now believed to be extinct [[baiji]] of the Yangtze River. He may be the only researcher to have worked with both the baiji and the presently highly endangered [[vaquita]], or [[Gulf of California]] harbor porpoise of the northern Gulf of California, Mexico. Besides working with river dolphins in Peru and China, Würsig has worked with oceanic whales in Argentina, far east Russia, and the Arctic; and a host of delphinids from the Bahamas<ref name="Norris" /> to Patagonia Argentina,<ref>Lichter AA. 1992. Tracks in the Sand, Shadows on the Sea: Marine Mammals of Argentina and Antarctica. Ediciones Terra Nova, Buenos Aires. 287 pp.</ref> from north-central California to Hong Kong and South Island New Zealand.<ref name="Cahill" /> A summary of his research life, especially as related to social strategies, is presented by Grady (2003).<ref name="Grady" /> Much of his work has been collaborative, and he has published with students and colleagues on issues of multi-species interactions among pinnipeds and cetaceans, marine mammals and marine birds, and noise pollution and mitigative effects. His present work is with Indo-Pacific [[humpback dolphin]]s in Hong Kong, [[dusky dolphin]]s on the South Island of New Zealand, and western [[gray whale]]s of far east Russia, all collaboratively with graduate students.

=== Dolphin behavior and individual identification ===
Some of Würsig's early research examined bottlenose and dusky dolphins in the South Atlantic. In collaboration with Melany Carballeira Würsig, he published studies of the behavior and ecology of bottlenose and dusky dolphins in Argentine waters. Their research included observations of group organization and the use of natural markings to identify individual animals. A 1977 paper in Science described photographic determination of group size, composition, and stability in coastal bottlenose dolphins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Würsig |first1=Bernd |last2=Würsig |first2=Melany |title=The Photographic Determination of Group Size, Composition, and Stability of Coastal Porpoises ( ''Tursiops truncatus'' ) |journal=Science |date=1977 |volume=198 |issue=4318 |pages=755–756 |doi=10.1126/science.198.4318.755 |bibcode=1977Sci...198..755W }}</ref>

=== Theodolite tracking and behavioral ecology ===
Würsig also helped develop the use of theodolites for tracking marine mammals from land. The technique enabled researchers to record the movements and behavior of cetaceans over relatively large areas without attaching instruments to the animals. His research used such observations to examine movement patterns, group behavior, habitat use, and responses to environmental conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Theodolite Tracking in Marine Mammal Research: From Roger Payne to the Present |url=https://www.aquaticmammalsjournal.org/article/vol-44-iss-6-piwetz/}}</ref>

=== Hawaiian spinner dolphins ===
During his postdoctoral research at the University of California, Santa Cruz, Würsig studied Hawaiian spinner dolphins. This work contributed to his continuing interest in the relationship between social behavior, habitat, and ecological conditions in cetaceans. His subsequent work with other researchers examined spinner dolphin grouping and population structure in Hawaiian waters.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Norris |first1=Kenneth S. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1525/j.ctt1pnxxv |title=The Hawaiian Spinner Dolphin |last2=Würsig |first2=Bernd |last3=Wells |first3=Randall S. |last4=Würsig |first4=Melany |last5=Brownlee |first5=Shannon M. |last6=Johnson |first6=Christine M. |last7=Solow |first7=Jody |last8=Wardrip |first8=Jenny |date=1994 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-08208-3 |jstor=10.1525/j.ctt1pnxxv }}</ref>

=== Dusky dolphins ===
In 2010, he and Melany Würsig published ''The Dusky Dolphin: Master Acrobat off Different Shores'', a detailed account of the species' biology and behavior. The book brought together observations from different populations and examined the species' social behavior, ecology, feeding strategies, and interactions with its environment.<ref name="Reference-2" />

Research involving Würsig has also examined dusky dolphin habitat use in New Zealand's Kaikoura region, including relationships between dolphin distribution and mussel farming. A study published in the New Zealand Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research in 2025 analyzed habitat use in a mussel-farming region and changes over time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Piwetz |first1=Sarah |last2=Pearson |first2=Heidi C. |last3=Honkus |first3=Krysta A. |last4=Würsig |first4=Bernd |title=Dusky dolphin (Lagenorhynchus obscurus) habitat use in a mussel farming region and changes over time |journal=New Zealand Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research |date=2025 |volume=59 |issue=2 |pages=418–440 |doi=10.1080/00288330.2024.2334287 |bibcode=2025NZJMF..59..418P |s2cid=278586076 }}</ref>

Bernd Würsig and his wife Melany Würsig first described the lives of [[dusky dolphin]]s, with day/night, seasonal, and overall habitat use patterns.<ref>Evans PGH. 1987. The Natural History of Whales and Dolphins. Pp. 177-178. Facts On File Publications, NY.</ref> They then went on to describe foraging strategies of dusky dolphins that herd anchovy and communicate with each other within and between groups,<ref>Griffin DR. 1992. Animal Minds. P. 61. University of Chicago University Press, Chicago, IL.</ref> with an important communication mode apparently mediated by leaping.<ref name="Cahill" /><ref>Connor RC, Peterson DM. 1994. The Lives of Whales and Dolphins. P. 39. Henry Holt and Co, NY.</ref>

Bernd and Melany Würsig also developed detailed non-invasive photographic recognition of dolphins,<ref name="Norris" /> a technique now used by hundreds of researchers worldwide,<ref name="Samuels">Samuels A, Tyack PL. 2000. Flukeprints: A history of studying cetacean societies. Pp. 36-37 In: Cetacean Studies: Field Studies of Dolphins and Whales. J Mann, RC Connor, PL Tyack, H Whitehead (eds). University of Chicago Press, Chicago IL.</ref> and discovered that [[common bottlenose dolphin]]s, have an “open” social system of ever-changing affiliations of individuals in groups and subgroups,<ref>Gaskin D.E. 1982. The Ecology of Whales and Dolphins, Pp. 128-129. Heinemann Press, London UK.</ref> a now commonly-accepted concept for many species and populations.

=== Bowhead whales ===
Würsig studied bowhead whales along the northslope of Alaska and eastern Canada in the 1980s-1990s, with much work on migrations and strategies of feeding and social/sexual relationships. This work has been put into context with more recent discoveries.<ref name="Cahill" />

Würsig also accepted two ideas of the great biologist Roger Payne, his field mentor during Ph.D. work, and expanded these throughout much of his own research.  One was the development of theodolite tracking of near-shore cetaceans and boats;<ref name="Norris" /><ref>Gailey G, Ortega-Ortiz JG. 2002. A computer-based system for cetacean theodolite tracking. Journal of Cetacean Research and Management 4(2):213-218.</ref> the other was identification photos and behavioral descriptions of animals from circling aircraft,<ref name="Samuels" /> with which much behavioral description of [[bowhead whale]]s, was facilitated by Würsig in the U.S. and Canadian Arctic.<ref>Burns JJ, Montague JJ, Cowles CJ. 1993. The Bowhead Whale. Society for Marine Mammalogy Special Publication, Allen Press, Lawrence KS.</ref> This work led to detailed descriptions of surface foraging and social behavior, as well as the fact that bowhead whales at times feed on bottom-dwelling organisms.<ref>Wells RS, Boness DJ, Rathbun GB. 1999. Behavior. Pp. 356-357 In: Biology of Marine Mammals. Reynolds JE III, SA Rommel (eds). Smithsonian Institution Press, Washington, DC.</ref>

=== Gray whales ===
Würsig has participated in long-term studies of western gray whales off Sakhalin Island, Russia. Research conducted with colleagues used boat-based photographic identification to investigate seasonal occurrence, annual return, and site fidelity. The study identified individual whales across multiple years and found repeated use of the region as a feeding ground.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Würsig |first1=Bernd |last2=Wells |first2=Randall S. |last3=Croll |first3=Donald A. |date=1986 |title=Behavior of gray whales summering near St. Lawrence Island, Bering Sea |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/abs/10.1139/z86-091 |journal=Canadian Journal of Zoology |publisher=NRC Research Press |volume=64 |issue=3 |pages=611–621 |doi=10.1139/z86-091 |bibcode=1986CaJZ...64..611W |issn=0008-4301}}</ref>

=== Human disturbance and underwater noise ===
Würsig and several colleagues developed and tested a bubble curtain system to reduce underwater industrial noises,<ref name="Cahill" /><ref name="Rsig">Würsig B, Greene CR, Jefferson TA. 2000. Development of an air bubble curtain to reduce underwater noise of percussive piling. Marine Environmental Research 49:79–93.</ref> and this technique has more recently received much engineering<ref>Spence J, Fischer R, Bahtiarian M, Boroditsky L, Jones N, Dempsey R. 2007. Review of existing and future potential treatments for reducing underwater sound from oil and gas industry activities. Noise Control Engineering Report 07-001, 185 pp. http://www.soundandmarinelife.org/Site/Products/NCE07-001_TreatmentsForUnderwaterSoundFromOil.pdf{{Dead link|date=June 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> and environmental<ref>Reyff JA. 2009. Reducing underwater sounds with air bubble curtains: Protecting fish and marine mammals from pile-driving noise. Transportation Research news, 262, May–June, pp. 31-33.  http://onlinepubs.trb.org/onlinepubs/trnews/trnews262rpo.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100705221157/http://onlinepubs.trb.org/onlinepubs/trnews/trnews262rpo.pdf |date=2010-07-05 }}</ref> attention. The study, published in ''Marine Environmental Research'' in 2000, found that the bubble curtain significantly reduced broadband noise pulse levels at measured distances from the pile-driving operation. The work was conducted in waters inhabited by Indo-Pacific humpback dolphins.<ref name="Rsig" />

=== Marine mammal conservation ===
Würsig's behavioral research has frequently been linked to conservation questions. His studies have examined how knowledge of animal behavior, habitat use, population structure, and human disturbance can inform the management of marine mammal populations.<ref name="www.dolphinbiology.org-1">{{Cite web |title=Dolphin Biology and Conservation |url=https://www.dolphinbiology.org/people/bernd_wursig.htm |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=www.dolphinbiology.org}}</ref>

His research on western gray whales, for example, documented the repeated use of feeding grounds and individual site fidelity, information relevant to understanding the importance of particular habitats for endangered populations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gailey |first1=Glenn |last2=Würsig |first2=Bernd |last3=McDonald |first3=Trent L. |date=2007 |title=Abundance, behavior, and movement patterns of western gray whales in relation to a 3-D seismic survey, Northeast Sakhalin Island, Russia |journal=Environmental Monitoring and Assessment |volume=134 |issue=1–3 |pages=75–91 |doi=10.1007/s10661-007-9812-1 |issn=0167-6369 |pmc=2798038 |pmid=17616825 |bibcode=2007EMnAs.134...75G }}</ref>

== Books and editorial work ==
Würsig has published about 200 peer review manuscripts, but the most important are probably those that first described results of individual recognition of dolphins by dorsal fin markings,<ref>Würsig B, Würsig M. 1977. The photographic determination of group size, composition and stability of coastal porpoises, ''Tursiops truncatus''. Science 198:755–756.</ref><ref>Würsig B. 1978. Occurrence and group organization of Atlantic bottlenose porpoises (''Tursiops truncatus'') in an Argentine Bay. Woods Hole Biological Bulletin 154:348–359.</ref> theodolite tracking,<ref>Würsig B., Würsig M. 1979. Behavior and ecology of the bottlenose dolphin, ''Tursiops truncatus'', in the South Atlantic. U.S. Fishery Bulletin 77(2):399–412.</ref><ref>Würsig B., Würsig M. 1980. Behavior and ecology of the dusky dolphin, ''Lagenorhynchus obscurus'', in the South Atlantic. U.S. Fishery Bulletin 77(4):871–890.</ref> and the development of a bubble curtain system to lower the intensity of stationary underwater industrial noises.<ref name="Rsig" /> Würsig co-wrote or co-edited books on the biology of spinner dolphins,<ref>Norris KS, Würsig B, Wells RS, Würsig M, eds. 1994. The Hawaiian Spinner Dolphin. University of California Press, Berkeley, CA. 408 pp.</ref> marine mammals of the [[Gulf of Mexico]],<ref>Würsig B, Jefferson TA, Schmidly DJ. 2000. The Marine Mammals of the Gulf of Mexico, Texas A&M University Press, College Station, TX. 232 pp.</ref> an encyclopedia of marine mammals,<ref>Perrin WF, Würsig B, Thewissen JGM. 2002. The Encyclopedia of Marine Mammals. Elsevier/Academic Press, San Diego, CA. 1414 pp.</ref><ref>Perrin WF, Würsig B, Thewissen JGM. 2009. The Encyclopedia of Marine Mammals, 2nd Edition. Elsevier/Academic Press, San Diego, CA. 1316 pp.</ref><ref>Würsig B, Thewissen JGM, Kovacs K. 2018. The Encyclopedia of Marine Mammals, 3rd Edition. Elsevier/Academic Press, San Diego, CA. 1157 pp.</ref> biology of dusky dolphins,<ref name="Reference-2">Würsig B, Würsig M. 2010. The Dusky Dolphin: Master Acrobat off Different Shores. Academic/Elsevier Press, Amsterdam. 441 pp.</ref> and a “coffee table” illustrated National Geographic book on whales and dolphins.<ref>Darling J, Nicklin C, Norris KS, Whitehead H, Würsig B. 1995. Whales, Dolphins, and Porpoises, National Geographic Society Press, Washington, DC. 232 pp.</ref>  He has written much on behavior and behavioral ecology of cetaceans, with a 1989 summary paper in the journal [[Science (journal)|Science]], and popular publications in [[Scientific American]], 1979, 1988. In 1999 Würsig coauthored a paper with international colleagues and former students David Weller and [[Amanda Bradford]] on the seasonal patterns of the western gray whales off [[Sakhalin Island]] in Russia.<ref>Weller DW, Würsig  B, Bradford AL, Burdin AM, Blokhin SA, Minakuchi H, Brownell RL. 1999. Gray whales (''Eschrichtius robustus'') off Sakhalin Island, Russia: seasonal and annual patterns of occurrence. Marine Mammal Science 15(4):1208–1227.</ref> He co-published a monograph on social ecology of delphinids, with Shannon Gowans and Leszek Karczmarski.<ref>Gowans S, Würsig B, Karczmarski L. 2007. The social structure and strategies of delphinids: predictions based on an ecological framework. Advances in Marine Biology 53(7):195-294.</ref> Würsig and the marine mammal program he founded are mentioned in a book on Texas A&M at Galveston.<ref name="Curley">Curley S. 2005. Aggies by the Sea. Texas A&M University at Galveston. Galveston, TX. 236 pp.</ref> He published an updated monograph on the marine mammals of the Gulf of Mexico.<ref name="Reference-1">Würsig B. 2017. Marine Mammals of the Gulf of Mexico, pp. 1489-1587, In: Habitats and Biota of the Gulf of Mexico: Before the Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill, Vol. II, ed. by H. Ward. Springer Open. {{ISBN|978-1-4939-3456-0}} (eBook)</ref> Würsig series-edited seven books by Springer Nature, Heidelberg Germany, on ethology and behavioral ecology of 1) odontocetes,<ref>Würsig B (editor) 2019. Ethology and Behavioral Ecology of Odontocetes, Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref> 2) sea otter and polar bear,<ref>Davis RW, Pagano AM (editors) 2021. Ethology and Behavioral Ecology of Sea Otters and Polar Bears,  Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref> 3) eared seals and walrus,<ref>Campagna C, Harcourt R (editors) 2021. Ethology and Behavioral Ecology of Otariids and the Odobenid, Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref> 4) true (or "earless") seals,<ref>Costa DP, McHuron EA (editors) 2022. Ethology and Behavioral Ecology of Phocids, Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref> 5) sirens, or manatees and the dugong,<ref>Marsh H (editor) 2022. Ethology and Behavioral Ecology of Sirenia, Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref> 6) mysticetes<ref>Clark CW, Garland EC (editors) 2022. Ethology and Behavioral Ecology of Mysticetes, Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref> and 7) a discussion of human-caused problems and potential solutions, "Marine Mammals; The Evolving Human Factor" with [[Giuseppe Notarbartolo di Sciara]].<ref>Notarbartolo di Sciara G, Würsig B (editors) 2022. Marine Mammals: The Evolving Human Factor, Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref> In 2023, Würsig and Mridula Srinivasan co-edited ''Social Strategies of Carnivorous Mammalian Predators: Hunting and Surviving as Families''. The book compares social hunting and survival strategies among several carnivorous mammals and considers how social behavior and ecology affect responses to natural and human-induced threats.<ref>Würsig B, Orbach D (editors) In prep. Sex in Cetaceans: Morphology, Behavior, and the Evolution of Sexual Strategies, Springer Nature, Cham Switzerland.</ref>
